title: Doze, Standby, Alarms & Background Limits
scopeHtml: Scope: platform power management (Doze, App Standby buckets, background execution limits), AlarmManager, battery-optimization exemptions, OEM killers, FCM priority, JobScheduler at platform level. WorkManager API usage belongs to A5; service/FGS mechanics to chunk 08.

notes.title: Doze mode and how to test it
notes.html:
The idea. When a phone lies still on a table at night, Android stops letting apps wake it up whenever they like. Instead it opens short "maintenance windows" where everyone gets to do their pending work together, then goes back to sleep. That saves a lot of battery.

Mechanism. Deep Doze (API 23) starts when the device is unplugged, stationary and screen-off for a while. While in Doze the system defers: network access, wakelocks, standard alarms (set, setExact), JobScheduler/WorkManager jobs, syncs and Wi-Fi scans. Maintenance windows come with growing gaps (roughly minutes at first, later hours; the idle interval grows exponentially, confirm numbers per version). API 24 added Light Doze: it kicks in when the screen is off and the device is unplugged, even while moving (for example in a pocket), with shorter, earlier windows.

screen off + unplugged --> LIGHT idle (cycles) 
                                |  stationary too
                                v
                       DEEP idle: [sleep ...... window] [sleep .......... window] ...
                       (gaps grow)  apps may run only in windows
 any motion / screen on / charger --> exits Doze

States are tracked by DeviceIdleController in system_server. Alarms that are allowed in Doze: setAndAllowWhileIdle() / setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() (rate limited, about one per 9 minutes per app, confirm), setAlarmClock(). High-priority FCM messages briefly whitelist the app for network.

Testing (ambiguous requirement: "make sure it works in Doze"). Define what must work: reminder fires, message arrives, sync completes at next window. Then:

adb shell dumpsys battery unplug
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle        # deep Doze
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle light  # light Doze (API 24+)
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle step              # step through states
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle unforce
adb shell dumpsys battery reset
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle whitelist +<pkg>  # add to allow list

Verify with adb shell dumpsys alarm and dumpsys jobscheduler. Real devices differ: OEM power managers add their own restrictions on top, so test on at least one Samsung/Xiaomi device and one Pixel.

Industry examples. WhatsApp and Gmail avoid polling and rely on high-priority FCM during Doze. Alarm Clock Xtreme and Google Clock use setAlarmClock. Fitness apps log from the sensor batch rather than staying awake.

Analogy. A school bus that stops running during the night and runs only a few scheduled times; the gaps between buses get longer the longer nobody rides.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Doze applies when the screen is off but the phone is charging. Charging exits it.
  • Believing the emulator and a real device behave identically; OEM layers vary.
  • Using wakelocks as a Doze workaround. Doze ignores them.

notes.title: AlarmManager basics
notes.html:
The idea. AlarmManager is the system's wake-up clock for your app: "run this PendingIntent at time T" even if your process is dead.

Mechanism. Types: RTC (wall-clock) vs ELAPSED_REALTIME (since boot, not affected by clock changes), each with _WAKEUP variant to wake the CPU. Methods: set (inexact on API 19+, batched), setExact, setWindow, setRepeating (inexact since 19), setInexactRepeating, setAndAllowWhileIdle, setExactAndAllowWhileIdle, setAlarmClock (shows the alarm icon, highest priority, permitted in Doze). The target is a PendingIntent (broadcast, service, or activity). Alarms are lost on reboot, force stop, and (for exact alarms) permission revocation, so re-register on BOOT_COMPLETED/LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED, app update (MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED) and permission-state change. A broadcast receiver fired by an alarm gets about 10 seconds in onReceive (foreground broadcast) before ANR risk; use goAsync() or hand over to WorkManager/expedited work, never do long work.

Spot-the-bug. Code:

am.setRepeating(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, firstTime, 60_000, pi)   // expects exactly every minute

Bugs: setRepeating is inexact since API 19 and minimum interval is clamped to about a minute for inexact; Doze defers it; PendingIntent created without FLAG_IMMUTABLE crashes on targetSdk 31; without BOOT_COMPLETED it never returns after a reboot; RTC breaks when the user changes timezone or clock. Fix: use setExactAndAllowWhileIdle chain rescheduling inside the receiver (set the next alarm each time), or WorkManager periodic (minimum 15 minutes) when exactness is not required.

Industry examples. Calendar/reminder apps and medication apps; alarm clocks; Telegram uses alarms only as a backup; many apps use alarms to trigger a high-priority notification to the user.

Analogy. Asking the hotel front desk for a wake-up call at 7:00; if the hotel loses power (reboot), the call is forgotten unless you ask again.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting set() or setRepeating() to be exact on modern Android.
  • Not re-registering after reboot.
  • Doing work in onReceive beyond a few seconds.

notes.title: Exact alarm permissions and Doze exemptions
notes.html:
The idea. Exact alarms are a battery risk, so the OS asks "is this really an alarm clock or calendar?", and also gives them special treatment inside Doze.

Mechanism. SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM (API 31; user-controlled special permission, see the behaviour-change notes) and USE_EXACT_ALARM (API 33; automatic, for alarm clock/timer/calendar apps and reviewed by Play). On API 33+ using neither throws SecurityException for exact APIs (including setExact, setExactAndAllowWhileIdle; setAlarmClock remains available as it is user-visible). Check canScheduleExactAlarms(); listen to ACTION_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED. The user can revoke in Settings, which cancels existing exact alarms.

Doze exemptions: setAlarmClock alarms wake the device and let the app run briefly; ...AllowWhileIdle alarms are allowed but throttled (about once per 9 minutes per app in Doze, confirm in docs); standard set/setExact are deferred to the next window. An exact alarm firing also gives a short allowance to start a foreground service (an exempt "background start" reason).

Industry examples. Google Clock uses USE_EXACT_ALARM; Todoist/TickTick reminders ask for the special access on newer OS.

Analogy. Emergency vehicles may skip the night curfew, ordinary delivery vans wait for the next gate opening, and the bell for the town hall needs a licence.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking setExact fires on time in Doze. It does not; only setExactAndAllowWhileIdle/setAlarmClock do.
  • Using USE_EXACT_ALARM for any reminder feature.
  • Forgetting to handle the permission being revoked.

notes.title: App Standby Buckets
notes.html:
The idea. Android sorts apps by how recently and how much the user uses them, and gives busier apps more freedom. An app you never open gets throttled hard.

Mechanism. API 28 buckets (UsageStatsManager STANDBY_BUCKET_*): ACTIVE, WORKING_SET, FREQUENT, RARE, and (API 30) RESTRICTED; also EXEMPTED (system) and NEVER. Machine-learning-assisted prediction decides. Effects (approximate; confirm current numbers): jobs run within quotas (ACTIVE: unconstrained; WORKING_SET about 10 min of runtime per 2 h; FREQUENT about 10 min per 8 h; RARE about 10 min per 24 h; RESTRICTED once a day, short); alarms limited (RARE one per 2 hours, etc.); FCM high-priority message budget (ACTIVE and WORKING_SET get priority; RARE/RESTRICTED are limited to a few per day; after Android 12 bucket affects the priority-message handling). Query with usageStatsManager.appStandbyBucket (API 28) and dumpsys usagestats; force with adb shell am set-standby-bucket <pkg> rare.

Production incident. A news app's morning sync worked for engaged users but silently failed for lapsed ones. Crashlytics was clean; WorkManager metrics showed jobs queued for 12 to 20 hours for users in RARE. The "daily at 7 am notification" arrived at noon. Fix: stop relying on jobs for time-critical delivery; send a high-priority FCM notification from the server, record the bucket in analytics (appStandbyBucket at session start) to see the distribution, offer a "bring back" flow; accept that RARE apps should not do much background work.

Industry examples. Games and utility apps are typically RARE; WhatsApp is ACTIVE for most users.

Analogy. A school that gives front-row seats to students who attend often and puts rarely seen ones at the back with tighter rules.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the bucket is chosen by the developer. It is chosen by the system.
  • Testing only on a freshly used phone, always ACTIVE.
  • Not distinguishing the RESTRICTED bucket (user-restricted battery) from RARE.

notes.title: Background execution limits (API 26)
notes.html:
The idea. In Android 8 the OS stopped letting apps run services and listen to implicit broadcasts in the background. Work has to be scheduled properly.

Mechanism.

  • Background services: once your app has been in the background for about a minute (grace period), the system stops its services. Starting a service with startService() from the background throws IllegalStateException (app is in background). startForegroundService() is the allowed path, and you must call startForeground() within about 5 seconds, otherwise ForegroundServiceDidNotCallStartForeground... / ANR-like crash ("Context.startForegroundService() did not then call Service.startForeground()").
  • Implicit broadcasts: most manifest-registered receivers for implicit broadcasts no longer work (for example CONNECTIVITY_ACTION, NEW_PICTURE). Exceptions remain (for example BOOT_COMPLETED, LOCALE_CHANGED, ACTION_PACKAGE_* family list). Register at runtime with registerReceiver when the app is running, or use ConnectivityManager.registerNetworkCallback and JobScheduler constraints.
  • Location updates in the background are throttled to a few per hour. Alternatives: JobScheduler / WorkManager, FCM, exact alarms, foreground services with notification.

Industry examples. Apps that kept a permanent service (older Facebook, Truecaller call-screening, BLE trackers) moved to FCM and WorkManager; ride apps use FGS only during a trip.

Analogy. A shop that no longer lets staff wander into the back room after closing; they have to book a task with the manager.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a started service keeps running forever after you go to background.
  • Registering for CONNECTIVITY_ACTION in the manifest.
  • Forgetting the 5-second startForeground deadline, including when onCreate is slow.

notes.title: FCM priority and Doze
notes.html:
The idea. A push notification can wake a sleeping phone, but only if the sender marks it urgent, and only a limited number of times.

Mechanism. FCM messages have priority: high (delivered immediately; wakes the device in Doze; gives the app a short temporary allowance to run, to start a foreground service and use the network for about 10 seconds) and normal (delivered at the next maintenance window, can be batched). Use high only when the user must see it now (chat, call, ride). Normal data messages do not guarantee delivery during Doze. Since Android 7 the platform may down-prioritise: if a high-priority data message does not produce a user-visible notification, FCM can reduce the app's priority. An android.priority in the message and notification messages (system displayed) vs data messages (your onMessageReceived) behave differently: notification messages are displayed even if the process is dead; data messages invoke your service, which then has about 20 seconds of work (use WorkManager for more). Time to live (ttl) and collapse_key control retention. In standby buckets RARE/RESTRICTED, high-priority messages are capped.

Industry examples. WhatsApp and Telegram use high-priority data messages and show the notification immediately; Uber's ride-acceptance and Google Meet's call use high priority; marketing pushes are normal.

Analogy. An urgent telegram is delivered at your door at once, while ordinary mail waits for the morning round.

Common interview traps.

  • Marking every push high; the system downgrades abusers.
  • Doing a long network sync in onMessageReceived rather than enqueueing work.
  • Assuming FCM works after the user force-stops the app. It does not until the app is opened.

notes.title: JobScheduler at the platform level
notes.html:
The idea. JobScheduler lets you say "run this when the network is on and the phone is charging" and the OS picks the right moment, batching jobs from many apps.

Mechanism. API 21. Build a JobInfo with constraints (setRequiredNetworkType, setRequiresCharging, setRequiresDeviceIdle, setRequiresBatteryNotLow, setRequiresStorageNotLow, addTriggerContentUri), timing (setPeriodic min 15 min with flex, setMinimumLatency, setOverrideDeadline), and setPersisted(true) (needs RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED). The system binds your JobService; onStartJob runs on the main thread (return true if work continues on another thread and call jobFinished), onStopJob is called when constraints fail or the system stops you, so work must be restartable. Job limits: about 10 minutes runtime per execution (in older versions); a limit of 100 jobs per app (API 24+, IllegalStateException beyond that on API 31+). Android 12 added setExpedited (quota-limited), Android 13/14 setUserInitiated (UIDT) with a foreground notification, JobService.setNotification. WorkManager sits on top of JobScheduler (API 23+) and adds backoff, chaining, unique work, observability; use it by default, and JobScheduler directly only in system-level or library code.

Industry examples. Chrome and Google Photos backups use JobScheduler/WorkManager with Wi-Fi + charging constraints; Netflix and Spotify downloads use constraints plus foreground work.

Analogy. A cleaning crew that visits when the building is quiet and the water is on, serving many offices in one round.

Common interview traps.

  • Doing heavy work on the main thread in onStartJob.
  • Using a periodic interval below 15 minutes (it is clamped).
  • Forgetting jobs are throttled by standby bucket and Doze.

notes.title: Battery optimization exemptions
notes.html:
The idea. Users can tell the system "do not limit this app". It is a big hammer that few apps deserve.

Mechanism. Settings.ACTION_REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS with REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS in the manifest asks the user to put the app on the Doze allow list. PowerManager.isIgnoringBatteryOptimizations(pkg) checks. When allowed: network access and wakelocks work during Doze, but alarms are still deferred unless using AllowWhileIdle, and standby/bucket and OEM kill rules may still apply. Google Play policy restricts it to apps whose core function breaks without it (messaging, VoIP, device automation, health companion); misuse leads to rejection. Alternatives: high-priority FCM, foreground service, ACTION_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATION_SETTINGS (the list screen, no policy issue). Android 12+ also has the "Restricted" battery state which no exemption can override.

Industry examples. Tasker, Home Assistant companion app and VPN/Bluetooth tracker apps (Tile) ask for it; most consumer apps do not.

Analogy. A VIP pass at the club: handed out sparingly, and it still does not let you skip the bouncer at the second door (OEM restrictions).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing it makes alarms exact.
  • Prompting it on first launch.
  • Forgetting the Play policy declaration.

notes.title: OEM background killers and the alarm incident
notes.html:
The idea. Some phone makers add their own aggressive "battery saver" that kills apps beyond what stock Android does. Your correct code may still not run.

Mechanism. Samsung (Device Care "sleeping apps"), Xiaomi/MIUI/HyperOS (Autostart, battery saver), Huawei (App launch), Oppo/Vivo/OnePlus (ColorOS/FuntouchOS/OxygenOS auto-launch, "deep optimization"), Realme and others kill the app on swipe-away, remove its alarms, block FCM when the app is "force stopped", or prevent boot receivers. Impacts: alarms vanish, jobs never run, FCM data messages not delivered, services stopped. The site dontkillmyapp.com tracks this. Mitigations: guide users to the vendor setting with a deep link (Intent to the vendor's auto-start screen, using try/catch and a generic fallback), ask the stock battery exemption, use foreground services for user-visible work, use high-priority FCM, detect kills (ApplicationExitInfo API 30+, reason REASON_USER_REQUESTED, REASON_OTHER, etc.; also a "heartbeat" timestamp comparison), and re-register alarms at launch and at every opportunity.

Production incident (OEM killers and alarms). A reminder app reported "alarms don't ring" on Xiaomi and Oppo only. Crashlytics showed nothing (nothing crashed). Telemetry showed AlarmManager registrations succeeded but the receiver never started. Fix: detect the vendor with Build.MANUFACTURER, show a one-time guide screen, use setAlarmClock (more privileged) rather than setExact, add a server-side FCM fallback that rings at the time, and track "alarm created vs alarm delivered" as a metric.

Industry examples. WhatsApp, Truecaller and Tile have OEM-specific help pages; Alarm apps ship per-vendor guides.

Analogy. A building with its own security guard who throws out visitors the city police (stock Android) already approved.

Common interview traps.

  • Blaming your code when nothing is logged. Check the exit reason and vendor first.
  • Assuming a foreground service survives OEM killers; many still kill it.
  • Hard-coding vendor intents without try/catch.

notes.title: Force stop, swipe away and system kill
notes.html:
The idea. The same app can "die" in three different ways, and they have very different consequences.

Event What happens Alarms FCM / broadcasts Services
Swipe from recents Task removed, process usually survives or is killed per OEM kept (stock) received may continue; onTaskRemoved for services
System (LMK) kill Process reclaimed for memory kept received; process restarts restarted if sticky
Force stop (Settings or am force-stop) App put in "stopped" state all cancelled blocked until the user launches the app again stopped
Uninstall/clear data everything removed removed removed removed

Stopped state: since Android 3.1 a stopped app receives no broadcasts, not even BOOT_COMPLETED, until the user launches it (or an explicit component start). Since API 30 apps can query ActivityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons to learn why a process died. Swiping on some OEMs acts like force stop (the OEM killer problem). Services with stopWithTask="false" survive task removal in stock Android.

Industry examples. Messaging apps are sensitive: a user who force-stops WhatsApp stops receiving messages until reopening.

Analogy. Closing a shop door for lunch (swipe), a power cut (system kill) and a shutter with a padlock only the owner can open (force stop).

Common interview traps.

  • Treating swipe-away as force stop on stock Android.
  • Assuming FCM wakes a force-stopped app.
  • Expecting onDestroy to run on process kill. It does not.

notes.title: Choosing the mechanism
notes.html:
The idea. There is no single best tool; the right choice depends on what must happen, when, and how visible it is to the user.

Need Use
Deferrable, must complete, survives reboot WorkManager (constraints, backoff)
Start now, short, user triggered Expedited WorkManager or a coroutine in a foreground UI
Long user-visible task (music, navigation, call, upload) Foreground service with the correct type
Long transfer started by user with progress User-initiated data transfer job (API 34)
Exact time user-visible (alarm, reminder) setAlarmClock / exact alarm with permission
Server-initiated, time-critical High-priority FCM
Reaction to system event while app is running Runtime-registered receiver, NetworkCallback

Design trade-off example. "Upload 200 photos in the background." WorkManager with network + battery-not-low constraints, chunked and resumable, with setForeground notification when the user started it; avoid a bare service (killed in Doze/App Standby); avoid exact alarms; tell the user via progress notification. Trade-offs: reliability vs immediacy vs battery vs user visibility.

Industry examples. Instagram uploads via WorkManager-like queues; Uber uses FGS during trips and FCM for dispatch; Google Photos uses constraints-based backup.

Analogy. Choosing between courier, post, phone call and a personal visit depending on urgency and importance.

Common interview traps.

  • Using an FGS for anything long-running "just in case".
  • Using alarms for periodic sync.
  • Ignoring that WorkManager is not exact.

notes.title: targetSdk migration post-incident review
notes.html:
The idea. A post-incident review is not about blame; it traces why an OS rule change reached users unnoticed, and what to change.

Worked example. Release bumps targetSdk 30 to 31. Two days later: reminders stop for ~8% of Android 12 users and ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException appears. Timeline: bump merged, no test on an Android 12 device with the app in the background; staged rollout reached 20%; alert on crash-free rate did not trigger because the reminder failure was silent for some paths. Root causes: (1) behaviour changes checklist not followed (exact alarm permission, FGS start restrictions, PendingIntent flags); (2) background paths not covered by CI; (3) no metric for "alarm fired vs scheduled". Fixes: restore exact alarm via canScheduleExactAlarms/fallback, move FGS start to allowed triggers, add an instrumented test using dumpsys deviceidle and am set-standby-bucket, add per-OS dashboards for background-work success, create a standard "targetSdk bump" checklist, halt rollout automatically on regression thresholds.

Analogy. After a road accident the city redesigns the junction, not just fines the driver.

Common interview traps.

  • Stopping at "we fixed the bug" without a detection and prevention action.
  • Looking only at crashes; silent failures matter more for background work.
  • Not breaking the rollout down by OS version.

notes.title: Evolution of background limits
notes.html:
The idea. Each Android release closes another loophole, so background work moved from "do anything" to "ask permission and be visible".

API 23 (6.0)  Doze, App Standby
API 24 (7.0)  Light Doze, background-optimization of implicit broadcasts (CONNECTIVITY)
API 26 (8.0)  Background service limit, implicit broadcast ban, notification channels
API 28 (9)    App Standby Buckets
API 29 (10)   Background activity starts blocked; background location needs its own permission
API 30 (11)   RESTRICTED bucket; permission auto-reset
API 31 (12)   FGS start from background banned; exact alarm permission; notification trampolines blocked
API 33 (13)   POST_NOTIFICATIONS; FGS Task Manager for users; USE_EXACT_ALARM
API 34 (14)   FGS types required; exact alarm denied by default; more restrictions on implicit intents
API 35 (15)   dataSync/mediaProcessing FGS timeouts; boot-time FGS restrictions
API 36 (16)   Tighter job quotas and stop-reason visibility

Notice the pattern: the OS moves toward user-visible or user-initiated work, batching, and explicit declarations. The lasting design advice: prefer WorkManager and FCM, keep foreground services short and typed, and treat any background work as best-effort.

Industry examples. WhatsApp, Gmail and Google Maps evolved from permanent services to FCM + foreground services only for active calls and navigation.

Analogy. A school that gradually adds rules: no running, then no phones, then permission slips.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up which release introduced which rule; remember the 26, 31, 34 and 35 landmarks.
  • Believing newer rules affect only apps targeting the new API; many apply to all apps.
  • Ignoring the trend and building the design on loopholes.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Doze and Light Doze defer jobs, alarms and network except in maintenance windows; ...AllowWhileIdle, setAlarmClock and high-priority FCM are the exceptions.
  • AlarmManager is inexact by default, lost on reboot and force stop, and exact versions require permission on modern Android.
  • Standby buckets (ACTIVE to RESTRICTED) throttle jobs, alarms and FCM budget; the system, not you, chooses the bucket.
  • API 26 banned background services and implicit broadcasts; use WorkManager, FCM or foreground services with a prompt startForeground.
  • Battery optimization exemptions are narrow in policy and do not defeat OEM killers or exact-alarm rules.
  • Force stop is not swipe-away: force stop cancels alarms and blocks FCM until the user reopens the app.
  • Choose the mechanism by urgency, visibility and survivability, test with dumpsys deviceidle and am set-standby-bucket, and measure silent failures in production.

questions.promptHtml: What is Doze mode? Explain light vs deep Doze, what it restricts, and what an app can still do.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every "my background work stopped overnight" bug traces back here. They want to see whether you know the conditions, the restrictions, and the escape hatches rather than just the word "Doze".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Doze is a battery saver the system enters when the device is idle. Deep Doze (API 23) needs screen off, unplugged and stationary for a while; light Doze (API 24) needs only screen off and unplugged. While dozing, the system defers network access, wake locks, standard alarms, JobScheduler jobs, syncs and Wi-Fi scans to periodic maintenance windows that get further apart over time. Exceptions are high-priority FCM, setAlarmClock, and setExactAndAllowWhileIdle/setAndAllowWhileIdle (rate-limited). Anything that must reach the user at a specific time has to use one of those.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
First principle: the biggest battery cost on an idle phone is apps waking the CPU and radio independently. Doze batches that: instead of N apps waking at random, the system lets everyone run together in a short window.

Deep Doze timeline (AOSP defaults; vendor/version may tune):
screen off + unplugged + still
   -> INACTIVE -> IDLE_PENDING -> SENSING -> LOCATING -> IDLE
   (device must stay still; a motion event resets back to ACTIVE)
IDLE:  |---- idle ----|M|------ longer idle ------|M|-------- ... |M|
        M = maintenance window (apps run jobs, syncs, deferred alarms)
        Interval between windows grows (roughly 1h -> 2h -> ... up to ~6h)

Light Doze (API 24+): screen off + unplugged, motion NOT required
   -> idle periods of minutes, short maintenance windows, grows less aggressively

What is restricted while idle (deep Doze; light Doze restricts a subset: network, jobs, syncs, alarms and wake locks, but not GPS/Wi-Fi scan):

  • Network access suspended.
  • Wake locks ignored.
  • Standard AlarmManager alarms (set, setExact, setRepeating) deferred to the next maintenance window.
  • Wi-Fi scans not performed; syncs and JobScheduler jobs deferred.
  • GPS and Wi-Fi scans ignored (deep Doze).

Allowed through:

  • High-priority FCM message (brief network + temporary allowlist).
  • setAlarmClock(), and setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() / setAndAllowWhileIdle() (system limits these per app, roughly once per 9 minutes in Doze per the docs).
  • Foreground services are not frozen by Doze network rules in practice for apps the user is actively using (visible notification), though OEMs differ.
  • Apps on the battery-optimization allowlist (isIgnoringBatteryOptimizations) keep network and wake locks, but not unlimited alarms.

Doze applies to all apps since API 23 regardless of targetSdk; it is an OS behavior, not an opt-in.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Check, don't assume. Exempt apps still go through standby buckets.
val pm = context.getSystemService(PowerManager::class.java)
val exempt = pm.isIgnoringBatteryOptimizations(context.packageName)
val dozing = pm.isDeviceIdleMode            // deep Doze
val light = pm.isDeviceLightIdleMode        // API 33+ public (hidden earlier)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "Doze is on API 23+ and kills my service": Doze does not kill; it withholds network, alarms and jobs. Process death is a separate mechanism.
  • Believing a partial wake lock keeps work running in Doze: the system ignores it for the duration.
  • Treating setRepeating as exact; since API 19 it is inexact, and in Doze it is deferred anyway.
  • Testing on a USB-connected, plugged-in phone and concluding Doze "doesn't happen".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you wake a dozing device at an exact time? → setAlarmClock() (or setExactAndAllowWhileIdle with the exact-alarm permission), accepting the rate limit for the latter.
  2. Why does a plugged-in phone never enter Doze? → Charging is one of the entry conditions; the device is considered active on power.
  3. How do you observe Doze transitions in the app? → Register for PowerManager.ACTION_DEVICE_IDLE_MODE_CHANGED (context-registered) and read isDeviceIdleMode; but design so you do not need to.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "Doze stops background work when the phone sits idle." The senior answer names the two tiers and their entry conditions, lists exactly which APIs are deferred vs exempt, explains why maintenance windows grow, and says the design response is to move time-critical delivery onto FCM high priority or alarm-clock-class alarms, not to fight Doze with wake locks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A messaging app's "typing indicator"-style socket stayed alive on the dev's plugged-in phones; on user devices at night the socket was silently throttled, and messages arrived only at the morning maintenance window until FCM high priority was added.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through AlarmManager: the alarm types, inexact vs exact, and what happens to alarms on reboot, app update and force stop.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Alarms are the lowest-level scheduling primitive. Weak candidates know setRepeating only; strong ones know the clock types, the inexact-by-default change, and the lifecycle gaps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: AlarmManager fires a PendingIntent at a time, outside my process lifetime. There are two clock bases, RTC (wall clock) and ELAPSED_REALTIME (since boot), each with a _WAKEUP variant that wakes the CPU. Since API 19 set and setRepeating are inexact so the system can batch them; setExact and friends need care and, from API 31, a permission. Alarms are wiped on reboot, on force stop, and on app update/uninstall, so I must reschedule from BOOT_COMPLETED and my own state.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Type Clock Wakes device? Use
RTC wall clock (System.currentTimeMillis) no, fires when next awake user-facing calendar time
RTC_WAKEUP wall clock yes reminders at "9:00 AM"
ELAPSED_REALTIME SystemClock.elapsedRealtime (incl. sleep) no "in 30 minutes"
ELAPSED_REALTIME_WAKEUP same yes timeouts that must fire
  • Use ELAPSED_REALTIME for relative delays: wall-clock alarms move if the user changes the time or timezone.
  • Inexact (set, setInexactRepeating, setWindow): the system may batch with other alarms; the window can be tens of minutes in Doze.
  • Exact (setExact, setExactAndAllowWhileIdle, setAlarmClock): fire at the requested time subject to Doze and permissions (see Q335, Q337).
  • Delivery: the PendingIntent (broadcast / service / activity) or an OnAlarmListener while the process is alive. A wakeup alarm holds a wake lock only for the duration of the broadcast onReceive; longer work needs goAsync(), a foreground service, or a job.
  • Lifetime: alarms live in system_server memory/state. They are cleared on reboot, on force stop (the package is stopped), and when the app is updated/uninstalled. They survive normal process death and swipe-from-recents on stock AOSP.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class BootReceiver : BroadcastReceiver() {
    override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) {
        if (intent.action == Intent.ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED ||
            intent.action == Intent.ACTION_MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED) {
            ReminderScheduler.rescheduleAll(context) // read from Room/DataStore
        }
    }
}
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED"/>
<receiver android:name=".BootReceiver" android:exported="true">
  <intent-filter>
    <action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED"/>
    <action android:name="android.intent.action.MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED"/>
  </intent-filter>
</receiver>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using RTC for "in 10 minutes": breaks on clock change.
  • Forgetting MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED, so every app update silently drops reminders. (Whether alarms survive an update is not something to rely on; reschedule.)
  • Reusing requestCode 0 for different alarms; PendingIntent identity ignores extras, so alarms overwrite each other.
  • Doing 30 s of work in onReceive.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why did the platform make set inexact in API 19? → Batching radio/CPU wakeups to save battery; apps targeting <19 stayed exact for compatibility.
  2. How do you cancel an alarm? → cancel() with an equal PendingIntent (same component/action/data/requestCode, extras ignored).
  3. What happens to alarms when the user force-stops the app? → Cleared, and the app receives no broadcasts until the user launches it again.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "setRepeating for periodic tasks". Senior: picks clock base by semantics, knows alarms are not durable state (persist the source of truth, reschedule on boot/replace/permission change), and keeps onReceive short.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A habit-tracker lost every reminder for ~40% of users after one release because the receiver only handled BOOT_COMPLETED, not MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED.

questions.promptHtml: What are App Standby buckets, how does an app move between them, and what do they limit?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It explains why the same code works for the developer (always active) and fails for users who open the app rarely, a very common production surprise.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since API 28 the system ranks each app by recent usage into Active, Working Set, Frequent, Rare, and (opt-in by the system) Restricted. The lower the bucket, the stricter the limits on job run time, alarm frequency and high-priority FCM. Using the app, interacting with its notification, or a foreground service moves it up; days of no use move it down. Apps can query their bucket but not set it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ACTIVE        - in foreground / just used (also notification interaction, FGS running)
WORKING_SET   - used regularly, e.g. daily
FREQUENT      - used often but not daily
RARE          - not used for days
RESTRICTED    - API 28+, system-assigned for abusive/battery-hungry apps (stricter still)
(NEVER = hidden bucket for installed-but-never-launched apps)

Buckets are assigned by usage-stats heuristics (and on Pixel by Adaptive Battery's ML model), not by a fixed day count; exact thresholds are device/OEM tunable. Effects (AOSP defaults; exact numbers live in DeviceConfig and change by release, verify on your target version):

  • Jobs: default runtime quota is about 10 min per window, with windows widening per bucket (order of 2 h Working set, 8 h Frequent, 24 h Rare; Restricted is roughly once a day). Active is effectively unlimited.
  • Alarms: allow-while-idle and non-exact alarms are quota-limited per hour per bucket (Active large, Rare ~1/hr).
  • FCM high-priority: the FCM docs describe per-bucket daily limits for Frequent/Rare; apps that never produce a user-visible notification get deprioritized.
  • Exempt: apps in the foreground, with a running foreground service, on the doze allowlist, device-admin/active, and some system roles (e.g. default dialer, SMS).

Query: UsageStatsManager.getAppStandbyBucket() (API 28) returns STANDBY_BUCKET_* constants. Listen with ACTION_APP_STANDBY_BUCKET_CHANGED (API 33 public).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val usm = context.getSystemService(UsageStatsManager::class.java)
val bucket = usm.appStandbyBucket
val tag = when (bucket) {
    UsageStatsManager.STANDBY_BUCKET_ACTIVE -> "active"
    UsageStatsManager.STANDBY_BUCKET_WORKING_SET -> "working_set"
    UsageStatsManager.STANDBY_BUCKET_FREQUENT -> "frequent"
    UsageStatsManager.STANDBY_BUCKET_RARE -> "rare"
    UsageStatsManager.STANDBY_BUCKET_RESTRICTED -> "restricted"
    else -> "other($bucket)"
}
analytics.setUserProperty("standby_bucket", tag) // segment crash/sync metrics by it
adb shell am get-standby-bucket com.example.app
adb shell am set-standby-bucket com.example.app rare

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Developing only on a daily-driver device that sits in Active.
  • Assuming a bucket is a fixed schedule: it is heuristic and OEM-modified.
  • Trying to "game" the bucket by launching an invisible activity; this is a policy violation and often does not count as interaction.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does a notification raise the bucket? → User interaction with a notification moves the app up (to at least Working Set); posting alone does not.
  2. What is Restricted bucket for? → Apps the system sees as consuming excessive resources or that the user restricted; very limited jobs and alarms, no BOOT_COMPLETED-style conveniences, FGS start limits.
  3. How would you make a sync design robust to buckets? → Treat bucket as telemetry, make sync cheap and server-driven (FCM), and tolerate hours/days of lag for background-only refresh.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names the five buckets. Senior: connects each bucket to concrete limits on jobs/alarms/FCM, instruments the bucket in analytics, and designs for the Rare device rather than the developer's phone.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "background refresh" feature showed 95% freshness in QA and 55% in the field; segmenting by standby bucket showed Rare/Frequent users were refreshing about once a day.

questions.promptHtml: What did Android 8.0 (API 26) change about background execution, and how does it differ from Doze?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates conflate Doze, standby and API 26 limits. A senior should separate "what the app is allowed to start" (26) from "what the system defers while idle" (Doze).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: From API 26, an app that is not in the foreground can't freely call startService(); it throws IllegalStateException once the app is "idle" (a minute or so after leaving the foreground), unless I use startForegroundService() and call startForeground() within about 5 seconds. Manifest-declared receivers also stopped getting most implicit broadcasts. Doze is different: it works on device idle state and defers network/alarms/jobs for every app. The limits depend on the app's state, Doze on the device's state.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The trigger is app state: the app has no visible activity, no foreground service, and isn't bound by a foreground client. The system gives a grace window of a few minutes (not a documented constant), after which background services are stopped and new startService() calls fail.
  • Allowed to start services from background (temporary allowlist, a few seconds): handling a high-priority FCM message, receiving a broadcast (onReceive window), executing a PendingIntent from a notification action, SMS/MMS delivery, VPN apps.
  • Implicit broadcasts: manifest receivers can't register for most implicit broadcasts (those without a specific package/component); exceptions include BOOT_COMPLETED, LOCALE_CHANGED, MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED, and others on the official exceptions list. Register at runtime when the process is alive, or use JobScheduler/WorkManager triggers.
  • Background location: fewer updates (a few per hour) for background apps from API 26; API 29/30 add background-location permission.
  • API 31 adds a stricter layer: starting a foreground service from background throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException unless an exemption applies (high-priority FCM, exact alarm callback, user-visible notification action, etc.). Chunk 08 covers FGS detail.
  • targetSdk vs OS: the service restrictions apply to apps targeting 26+; apps targeting lower had them enforced from API 26 only on a best-effort/whitelist basis. In practice, the Play requirement (target recent API) makes them universal.
App state          startService()           Alarm/Job/FCM
foreground         OK                       n/a
background <~1min  OK                       n/a
background idle    IllegalStateException    use startForegroundService / JobScheduler

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken in background on API 26+
context.startService(Intent(context, SyncService::class.java))

// Correct: a job (platform-scheduled), or FGS with a visible notification
val job = JobInfo.Builder(42, ComponentName(context, SyncJobService::class.java))
    .setRequiredNetworkType(JobInfo.NETWORK_TYPE_ANY)
    .build()
context.getSystemService(JobScheduler::class.java).schedule(job)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fixing the crash with startForegroundService() and a fake notification for a task that should be a job; this just moves the crash to the 5-second timeout.
  • Catching IllegalStateException and swallowing it: the work silently never happens.
  • Believing an exact alarm or notification keeps the app "foreground".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the same code work in the debugger? → The app is in the foreground or recently foregrounded; the failure appears after the idle grace period.
  2. How do you react to a broadcast like CONNECTIVITY_CHANGE now? → ConnectivityManager.registerNetworkCallback or a job with a network constraint.
  3. What is the difference between "background" and "cached"? → Background is process state with services; cached is empty/LRU process eligible for kill with no active components.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "can't start services in background; use WorkManager." Senior: knows the allowlist windows, the API 26 vs 31 FGS rules, the broadcast exceptions, and separates app-state limits from Doze/standby.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After bumping targetSdk to 26, a location-sync service crashed with Not allowed to start service Intent ... app is in background uid null for users who backgrounded the app, fixed by moving to a job plus a user-visible FGS only for active tracking.

questions.promptHtml: Explain SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM vs USE_EXACT_ALARM. When do you need each, what is the default state per Android version, and how do you handle revocation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is the most frequent targetSdk-migration trap for reminder/calendar apps and ties policy to platform behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since API 31, setExact* requires SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, a special app-access permission the user can toggle in Settings. For apps targeting 33+ and installed fresh on Android 14+, it's denied by default; on 12/13 it is granted by default. USE_EXACT_ALARM (API 33) is granted automatically at install and can't be revoked, but Play only permits it for core alarm-clock, timer or calendar apps. I check canScheduleExactAlarms() before scheduling, send the user to the settings page if needed, and re-schedule when the permission state changes, with an inexact fallback.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM USE_EXACT_ALARM
Introduced API 31 API 33
Grant Special access; user toggle; pre-granted on 12/13 upgrades; denied for new installs targeting 33+ on 14+ Install-time, not revocable
Play policy For apps where exactness is a user-facing feature Restricted to alarm clocks, timers, calendars (policy declaration)
If missing SecurityException from setExact* (targeting 31+) n/a
  • Revocation: if the user revokes SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM the system kills the app and cancels its exact alarms. On re-grant the system sends ACTION_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED to the app; I must reschedule.
  • setAlarmClock() doesn't need either permission (it shows the alarm icon and is user-visible) and is the escape hatch when I genuinely run an alarm-clock UX. Don't use it as a loophole for generic reminders; Play policy and users will punish it.
  • Inexact setAndAllowWhileIdle/setWindow need no permission.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun scheduleExact(ctx: Context, at: Long, pi: PendingIntent) {
    val am = ctx.getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < 31 || am.canScheduleExactAlarms()) {
        am.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, at, pi)
    } else {
        am.setWindow(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, at, 10 * 60_000L, pi) // degrade gracefully
        // prompt once, with explanation:
        ctx.startActivity(Intent(Settings.ACTION_REQUEST_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM)
            .setData(Uri.parse("package:${ctx.packageName}"))
            .addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK))
    }
}
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM"/>
<!-- or, only if Play approves your category: -->
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.USE_EXACT_ALARM"/>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring both permissions; on 13+ USE_EXACT_ALARM wins and you still need Play's declaration.
  • Not rescheduling after revoke and re-grant.
  • Assuming "upgrade preserves": users updating the app on 12/13 keep the grant; new installs on 14+ don't, so QA on upgraded devices misses the failure.
  • Using exact alarms for periodic sync (policy and battery abuse).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does the system do on revoke? → Stops the app and cancels its exact alarms.
  2. Can a background app request the permission? → No, it needs a user trip to Settings; call from a visible UI with a rationale.
  3. Where is the permission visible in adb? → adb shell appops get <pkg> SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM; set it with cmd appops set <pkg> SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM deny to test.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "need the permission for exact alarms." Senior: gives per-version defaults, policy constraint, revocation behavior, setAlarmClock distinction, and designs a degraded path when denied.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After targeting 33, a meditation app's reminders crashed with SecurityException: ... requires android.permission.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM for fresh installs on Android 14 devices only.

questions.contextHtml:
A medication-reminder app (200k DAU) schedules daily reminders. After a release targeting API 34, Crashlytics shows IllegalArgumentException: targetSdkVersion ... requires that one of FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE be specified on some paths, and support tickets say reminders "come late at night" or "vanish after phone restarts". Review:

object ReminderScheduler {
    fun schedule(ctx: Context, medId: Long, atMillis: Long) {
        val am = ctx.getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)
        val i = Intent(ctx, ReminderReceiver::class.java).putExtra("med", medId)
        val pi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(ctx, 0, i, 0)
        am.setExact(AlarmManager.RTC, atMillis, pi)
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find every defect and give the corrected version.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add FLAG_IMMUTABLE." That fixes the crash but leaves late alarms, overwritten reminders, lost-on-reboot, and a latent SecurityException.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are all reminders stored in a DB (source of truth)? Does the user expect exact times (medication = yes)? Is the app a declared alarm/calendar category for USE_EXACT_ALARM, or must it use SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM? Which OS versions fail (14+ fresh installs?).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: add FLAG_IMMUTABLE, unique request code, RTC_WAKEUP, and permission check; ship via staged rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) flags missing: crash on targetSdk 31+; (b) RTC not RTC_WAKEUP and setExact not allow-while-idle: deferred until the screen turns on or a maintenance window = "late at night"; (c) requestCode 0 shared: every schedule() replaces the previous alarm because PendingIntent equality ignores extras; (d) no BOOT_COMPLETED/PACKAGE_REPLACED reschedule; (e) no canScheduleExactAlarms() check: SecurityException for new installs on 14+.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell dumpsys alarm | grep -A5 com.example to see how many alarms exist (expect 1, not N); adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle then check delivery; reboot and re-run dumpsys alarm; appops set ... deny to reproduce the SecurityException; Crashlytics grouping by API level.
  5. Root cause: Several independent assumptions from pre-12 behavior: alarms are persistent, exact is free, flags are optional, one request code is fine.
  6. Fix:
object ReminderScheduler {
    fun schedule(ctx: Context, medId: Long, atMillis: Long) {
        val am = ctx.getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)
        val i = Intent(ctx, ReminderReceiver::class.java)
            .setAction("com.example.REMIND").setData(Uri.parse("med://$medId"))
            .putExtra("med", medId)
        val pi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(
            ctx, medId.hashCode(), i,
            PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE)
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < 31 || am.canScheduleExactAlarms()) {
            am.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, atMillis, pi)
        } else {
            am.setAndAllowWhileIdle(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, atMillis, pi)
        }
    }
}

Plus a boot/replace/exact-permission-changed receiver that reads all pending reminders from Room and calls schedule again, and ReminderReceiver that shows the notification and schedules the next occurrence (no setRepeating). 7. Prevention: Instrumented test per API level (31, 33, 34); lint (UnspecifiedImmutableFlag); a "reschedule on boot" test with adb reboot; a synthetic canary alarm to measure lateness. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not setRepeating (inexact, drifts); not a foreground service just to stay alive; not setAlarmClock for non-alarm UX since it puts an alarm icon in the status bar and has policy implications.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why use setData with a URI? → Distinguishes PendingIntents without relying on request-code hash collisions; hashCode() of a Long can collide, so Uri data is safer.
  • Medication must fire at an exact time even in Doze, is setExactAndAllowWhileIdle enough? → It is rate-limited roughly once per 9 min in Doze and OEM killers can still stop it; for a safety-critical case pair with setAlarmClock if Play category allows, plus a server fallback via high-priority FCM.
  • User changes timezone? → Listen for ACTION_TIMEZONE_CHANGED/ACTION_TIME_CHANGED and reschedule if reminders are wall-clock local.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A reminder app had "random" missing reminders for months. The root cause was a constant request code of 0: only the last scheduled medication ever fired, and QA tested a single reminder at a time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only fixes the flag crash.
  • Hire: also finds RTC_WAKEUP, the request-code collision and reboot reschedule.
  • Strong hire: adds exact-alarm permission handling, Doze verification via adb, per-API tests, and server-side fallback.

questions.promptHtml: Compare setAndAllowWhileIdle, setExactAndAllowWhileIdle, setAlarmClock and setWindow in the context of Doze. Which would you pick for a calendar reminder, a chat retry timer, and a wake-up alarm app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether the candidate knows that "exact" and "fires in Doze" are separate properties and that each API has a policy and rate-limit cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: setAlarmClock() is the strongest: exact, fires in Doze, shows an alarm icon, no exact-alarm permission, and the system exits Doze for it (reserved for real alarm UX). setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() is exact and works in Doze but needs the exact-alarm permission and is rate-limited (about once per 9 minutes per app in Doze). setAndAllowWhileIdle() fires in Doze but inexact and rate-limited. setExact/setWindow without AllowWhileIdle get deferred to maintenance windows. Calendar reminder: exact-and-allow-while-idle (or alarm clock if the app is a calendar category). Retry timer: inexact allow-while-idle or a job. Wake-up app: setAlarmClock.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
API Exact? Fires in Doze? Permission (API 31+) Visible to user
set / setWindow no deferred none no
setAndAllowWhileIdle no yes, rate-limited none no
setExact yes deferred SCHEDULE/USE_EXACT_ALARM no
setExactAndAllowWhileIdle yes yes, rate-limited SCHEDULE/USE_EXACT_ALARM no
setAlarmClock yes yes, no throttle for alarm clocks none alarm icon, getNextAlarmClock
  • Rate limits are enforced in AlarmManagerService: allow-while-idle alarms are limited per app in idle mode and per standby bucket when not idle; excess alarms are delayed, not dropped.
  • setAlarmClock takes an AlarmClockInfo with a "show" PendingIntent (shown when the user taps the status icon).
  • Repeating: schedule the next alarm from the receiver; setRepeating is inexact and not allow-while-idle.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val show = PendingIntent.getActivity(ctx, 1, Intent(ctx, AlarmListActivity::class.java),
    PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE)
am.setAlarmClock(AlarmManager.AlarmClockInfo(triggerAt, show), firePi)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Chaining setExactAndAllowWhileIdle every minute to emulate a periodic poll; throttled and flagged by vitals ("excessive wakeups").
  • Using setAlarmClock for non-alarms to dodge the permission.
  • Assuming "AllowWhileIdle" also makes the app network-reachable; network is still suspended until a maintenance window unless the app has a high-priority FCM allowlist.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What network access does the app have when the alarm fires in Doze? → Very brief; the receiver should post a notification or kick a job, not depend on a slow request.
  2. Why is setAlarmClock special? → The system treats it as user-visible, exits idle for it, and exposes it to the lock screen/clock UI.
  3. What does Android vitals call excessive wakeups? → Alarm wakeups above a threshold (documented as more than 10 per hour on average over a day) flag the app.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use setExactAndAllowWhileIdle." Senior: matches API to product semantics, explains rate limits and permissions, and refuses to turn alarms into a polling loop.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A timer app moved from setExact to setAlarmClock and the "alarms late in the morning on Pixels" tickets went to zero, at the cost of a status-bar alarm icon the PM had to sign off on.

questions.promptHtml: How do high-priority and normal-priority FCM messages behave in Doze and under App Standby, and what can the app do inside onMessageReceived?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Push is the only reliable wake path for server-driven work. They test whether you know its limits and the cost of misusing high priority.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Normal-priority messages are deferred during Doze until a maintenance window. High-priority messages wake the device, give brief network access and a short temporary allowlist so I can finish work (and, on API 31+, start a foreground service). I get roughly 10 seconds in onMessageReceived, so I post a notification or enqueue a job. High priority is meant to end in a user-visible notification; if it doesn't, FCM can downgrade future messages, and standby buckets cap how many high-priority messages an app gets per day in Frequent/Rare.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Server --FCM--> Google Play services (persistent connection, one per device)
                 |
   priority=normal: delivered at next window when idle (batched)
   priority=high  : delivered immediately; app gets temp allowlist
                 v
        FirebaseMessagingService.onMessageReceived  (~10 s budget)
  • Data vs notification messages: a notification-message is shown by the system tray when the app is in background (no app code runs); a data message always calls onMessageReceived. Use data messages with priority: high when you need code.
  • Allowed under the temp allowlist: start a FGS from background (API 31+), network, wake lock for the message duration. Not allowed: long-running work; hand off to JobScheduler/expedited work or a short FGS.
  • Standby buckets: FCM docs describe per-bucket quotas for high-priority messages; numbers are not a stable API, so I treat "Rare/Restricted gets throttled" as the contract.
  • Force-stopped apps (or Restricted/hibernated apps on newer versions) receive no messages until the user launches them again.
  • TTL (default 4 weeks) and collapse_key control queuing while the device is offline/dozing.
  • Device/OEM issues: some OEMs kill the process on swipe and drop pushes; see Q342.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
{
  "message": {
    "token": "<device token>",
    "android": { "priority": "high", "ttl": "60s", "collapse_key": "chat-42" },
    "data": { "type": "new_message", "chat": "42" }
  }
}
class MsgService : FirebaseMessagingService() {
    override fun onMessageReceived(m: RemoteMessage) {
        // < 10 s: persist, notify, enqueue follow-up. No long network here.
        notifier.show(m.data)
        WorkManagerFetch.enqueueExpedited(m.data["chat"]!!) // A5 covers WM details
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Marking every message high priority (analytics, silent syncs): gets downgraded and drains battery.
  • Relying on notification-messages when app code must run.
  • Doing the full sync in onMessageReceived and getting killed mid-way.
  • Ignoring onNewToken and sending to stale tokens.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A silent sync push never arrives overnight; why? → Normal priority in Doze, or high priority throttled because the app is in Rare and does not produce notifications.
  2. Does high priority bypass battery optimization toggles set by the user (Restricted)? → No; background-restricted or force-stopped apps may not receive it.
  3. How do you verify delivery? → FCM delivery report/BigQuery export, adb shell dumpsys activity service FirebaseMessagingService/logcat FirebaseMessaging, and the RemoteMessage.originalPriority vs priority.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "high priority ignores Doze." Senior: knows the downgrade rule, the data vs notification distinction, the ~10 s budget, the bucket quotas, the force-stop exception, and designs payload size/TTL/collapse to fit.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A food-delivery status feature set all pushes to high priority; Google throttled silent updates and "order picked up" pushes started arriving minutes late for Rare-bucket users until non-visible updates moved to normal priority plus polling on app open.

questions.promptHtml: At the platform level, how does JobScheduler decide when to run a job, and what constraints and limits does it enforce?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: WorkManager sits on JobScheduler on modern devices; understanding the platform layer explains constraints, quotas, 10-minute limit, and why a "constraint satisfied" job still doesn't run.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I describe a job with JobInfo (network type, charging, battery-not-low, storage-not-low, idle, content-URI triggers, latency/deadline, periodic interval) and the system runs it in my JobService when all constraints are met and quota allows, in a batch with other apps. onStartJob runs on the main thread, the job has about 10 minutes, then the system calls onStopJob, and I return true if I want a reschedule. Periodic jobs have a 15-minute minimum interval. Standby buckets, Doze and battery saver can delay it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Constraints: setRequiredNetworkType (ANY/UNMETERED/NOT_ROAMING/CELLULAR), setRequiresCharging, setRequiresBatteryNotLow, setRequiresStorageNotLow, setRequiresDeviceIdle, addTriggerContentUri, setMinimumLatency, setOverrideDeadline.
  • Execution: JobService.onStartJob() executes on the main thread; I must offload and call jobFinished(params, needsReschedule). Returning false means no async work.
  • Execution limit: roughly 10 minutes per run (older: 10 min for all), after which onStopJob is called with a stop reason (getStopReason() API 31).
  • Backoff: default exponential, 30 s initial, capped around 5 hours.
  • Periodic: setPeriodic(interval, flex); minimum interval 15 min, minimum flex 5 min; clamped silently.
  • Persisted jobs: setPersisted(true) needs RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED, survives reboot.
  • Quotas: running time per standby bucket (see Q333) and expedited job quotas (setExpedited, API 30+; behaves like a time-boxed, higher-priority job; since API 31 expedited jobs may need a notification when run as FGS-like) and user-initiated data transfer jobs (API 34, setUserInitiated(true) requires RUN_USER_INITIATED_JOBS, user-visible notification).
  • Batching: jobs often run in a shared window; that's why a job with a "network ANY" constraint can wait hours when the app is in Rare or Doze (it runs in maintenance windows).
JobInfo -> JobSchedulerService -> constraint trackers (battery, connectivity, idle, storage)
                                -> quota controller (bucket, expedited, FGS, top)
                                -> ready queue -> bind JobService -> onStartJob (main thread)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SyncJob : JobService() {
    private var job: kotlinx.coroutines.Job? = null
    override fun onStartJob(p: JobParameters): Boolean {
        job = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch {
            val ok = runCatching { repo.sync() }.isSuccess
            jobFinished(p, !ok) // reschedule with backoff on failure
        }
        return true // work continues off-thread
    }
    override fun onStopJob(p: JobParameters): Boolean { job?.cancel(); return true }
}

val info = JobInfo.Builder(1, ComponentName(ctx, SyncJob::class.java))
    .setRequiredNetworkType(JobInfo.NETWORK_TYPE_UNMETERED)
    .setRequiresBatteryNotLow(true)
    .setPeriodic(6 * 60 * 60_000L, 30 * 60_000L)
    .setPersisted(true)
    .build()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing network work in onStartJob directly (ANR / NetworkOnMainThreadException).
  • Expecting a periodic job to fire on the clock: it fires in the flex window at the end of each period, at the system's convenience.
  • Forgetting jobFinished, which keeps the job holding a wake lock until timeout.
  • Using JobScheduler with a constraint nobody satisfies (e.g. requiresDeviceIdle + charging), so it never runs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is a job delayed on a device in the Rare bucket? → Job execution quota is small and windowed per bucket.
  2. How do you debug a job that hasn't run? → adb shell dumpsys jobscheduler | grep -A20 <pkg> shows constraints satisfied/unsatisfied, bucket and quota state; cmd jobscheduler run -f <pkg> <jobId> forces it.
  3. When use expedited jobs? → Short user-initiated-ish work that should start quickly (e.g. send a message); quota-limited, so don't use for sync.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists constraints. Senior: explains main-thread callback, quota/bucket/Doze interplay, the 15-minute floor, how to debug with dumpsys jobscheduler, and when to prefer WorkManager vs raw JobScheduler (chunk A5).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A job using setRequiresDeviceIdle(true) + charging ran on 3% of devices because the idle state rarely coincided with charging; dropping the idle constraint raised success to 90%.

questions.promptHtml: What are battery-optimization exemptions in Android, how does an app request one, and when is it appropriate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Product teams often ask "just whitelist us". A senior must know the API, Play policy, the actual effect, and the alternatives.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An exemption puts the app on the Doze allowlist, so it keeps network and can hold partial wake locks in Doze and is less restricted by standby. I check isIgnoringBatteryOptimizations() and, if truly necessary, launch ACTION_REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS with the package URI (needs REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS), or send the user to ACTION_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATION_SETTINGS. Google Play restricts the direct-request intent to apps whose core function breaks without it (e.g. device automation, messaging/VoIP in some cases, companion/health devices). It is not a substitute for FCM, and OEM killers ignore it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Effect: allowlisted apps are not subject to Doze network/wakelock/job suppression the same way, but alarms are still rate-limited and standby bucket logic still applies in part (verify per version).
  • The user-facing UI is "Battery optimization" (Settings > Apps > Special access); on Android 12+/13+ some OEMs relabel it "Unrestricted" vs "Optimized" vs "Restricted" (Android 9+ per-app battery usage setting; Android 13 added more granular behaviour). Being "Unrestricted" is what survives most OEM killers.
  • Request flow:
App checks exemption -> not exempt -> show rationale screen -> system dialog (ACTION_REQUEST_...)
   -> user taps Allow -> app on allowlist (deviceidle whitelist)
  • Play policy: using REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS for apps not in a permitted category risks removal; the fallback is the settings list intent plus in-app instructions.
  • Alternatives that don't need exemption: FCM high priority, setAlarmClock, expedited jobs, user-visible foreground service.
  • dumpsys deviceidle whitelist lists system and user allowlisted packages.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun maybeAskForExemption(activity: Activity) {
    val pm = activity.getSystemService(PowerManager::class.java)
    if (pm.isIgnoringBatteryOptimizations(activity.packageName)) return
    // Policy: only if your core feature requires it; otherwise use the list screen.
    val i = Intent(Settings.ACTION_REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS)
        .setData(Uri.parse("package:${activity.packageName}"))
    activity.startActivity(i)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Prompting on first launch: users deny and Play reviewers reject.
  • Assuming exemption removes OEM background killing.
  • Using exemption to hide a polling design; battery vitals will still flag wakeups.
  • Not handling ActivityNotFoundException on exotic ROMs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does an exempt app still get Doze alarm deferral? → Standard alarms are still deferred/rate-limited; exempt apps retain network/wakelock access, not unlimited alarms.
  2. How would you detect the user later revoking it? → Re-check on resume; there's no broadcast guarantee, so also reflect it in a diagnostic screen.
  3. Alternative for a fitness tracker? → Foreground service of the right type with a notification, not an exemption.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "ask the user to disable battery optimization." Senior: weighs Play policy, product impact, alternatives, per-OEM settings, and builds a diagnostic/health screen instead of repeated nagging.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A VoIP app's call push arrived late for 8% of users; adding a one-time contextual exemption request (after the first missed call) halved the complaints, while OEM-specific autostart screens handled the remainder.

questions.contextHtml: QA files: "Notifications for scheduled tasks don't show up overnight on a Pixel 7 (Android 14), but work when I test at my desk." The app (1.2M DAU) uses an exact alarm to show a morning briefing at 07:00 plus an hourly WorkManager sync. Crash rate is fine (99.7% crash-free) and no ANRs. Engineering says "can't reproduce". Logs from a bug report show Alarm ... deferred is absent; the device was on a charger overnight at 03:00 but unplugged at 05:30.
questions.promptHtml: How do you reproduce and diagnose this, and what do you ask first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Can't repro; maybe it's the phone." Or "Add a wake lock." Neither tests the idle path.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the phone stationary and unplugged long enough for deep Doze (plugged in means no Doze)? What exactly didn't show: the 07:00 alarm or the sync result? Is the app battery setting "Optimized" or "Restricted"? Fresh install on 14 or upgraded (exact-alarm permission)? Which bucket (am get-standby-bucket)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed yet; collect a bug report immediately after the miss; for users, make sure the morning alarm uses the right API.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM denied on fresh Android 14 install, so the code fell back to inexact; (b) alarm is setExact without allow-while-idle, deferred to a maintenance window after 07:00; (c) bucket Rare because user rarely opens the app; (d) "Restricted" battery state set by the user/system; (e) red herring: charger at 03:00, since unplug at 05:30 means Doze may only have started shortly before 07:00.
  4. How I'd verify each:
adb shell dumpsys battery unplug
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle enable deep
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle        # enter deep Doze now
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle get deep          # expect IDLE
adb shell dumpsys alarm | grep -A6 com.example # type, window, flags
adb shell am set-standby-bucket com.example rare
adb shell cmd appops get com.example SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle unforce && adb shell dumpsys battery reset

Then schedule the alarm for 2 minutes ahead and watch logcat -s AlarmManager. Compare delivery with standard setExact vs setExactAndAllowWhileIdle vs setAlarmClock. 5. Root cause (typical): Fresh Android 14 install has the exact-alarm permission denied; the code's if (canScheduleExactAlarms()) swallowed the else branch, so no alarm was ever scheduled or an inexact window slipped far past 07:00. 6. Fix: Handle the denied branch (inexact allow-while-idle with a tight window, plus a rationale screen to grant the permission), and record the effective path in analytics ("exact_granted", bucket). 7. Prevention: A CI instrumented test running force-idle scenarios; a debug screen showing permission, bucket, battery state; alerting on alarm lateness telemetry (fired time minus scheduled time). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not wake locks (ignored in Doze), not foreground service overnight, not an exemption prompt as the first reaction.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• It fails only on Samsung phones; what changes? → OEM "sleeping apps" can drop alarms (Q342); verify with the device's battery settings, not AOSP commands.
  • Does force-idle reflect real deep Doze? → It enters IDLE state for testing but skips the motion/time heuristics; confirm with a real overnight run on a spare device.
  • How do you test light Doze? → dumpsys deviceidle force-idle light (where supported by the build).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team spent two sprints on "alarm bug" until someone noticed all affected users were on fresh installs: the permission default had changed from granted to denied and their upgrade-path QA devices all kept the grant.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests wake locks or can't produce an adb test plan.
  • Hire: reproduces with force-idle, checks permission and bucket.
  • Strong hire: ranks hypotheses by evidence (fresh vs upgraded install), adds telemetry for lateness and a CI check.

questions.promptHtml: Why do apps get killed or throttled on Xiaomi, Oppo/Vivo, Huawei and Samsung beyond stock Android's rules, and how do you design around it without hacks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A big share of Android reliability problems in India and emerging markets are OEM behaviors, not AOSP. Senior engineers must engineer for them professionally.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Many OEMs add proprietary task killers and "autostart/sleeping app/battery saver" layers on top of AOSP to win battery benchmarks. They may kill the process when it's swiped from recents (effectively force-stop, which cancels alarms and blocks pushes), block auto-start after boot, and throttle background work for apps not marked "unrestricted". I can't fix it in code. I design for it: rely on FCM high priority, make state recoverable, detect the likely problem from telemetry, and guide users to the right OEM setting with honest UX, without deep-linking undocumented settings blindly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The community reference is dontkillmyapp.com, which documents per-vendor behavior and has changed over time; treat it as a starting list, not a spec.
  • Typical mechanisms:
    • Swipe from recents performs force-stop semantics: alarms/jobs cleared, receivers off.
    • Autostart / "Auto-launch" toggles gate BOOT_COMPLETED and background launches (MIUI, ColorOS, FuntouchOS, EMUI).
    • Samsung "Sleeping apps"/"Deep sleeping apps": apps unused for a few days are put to sleep (no background activity until opened).
    • Aggressive RAM/"cleaner" tasks killing cached processes even with a foreground service on some builds.
  • What stays reliable: user-visible foreground service with ongoing notification (best effort), high-priority FCM (delivered by Play services, which are typically allowlisted unless the app is force-stopped), apps flagged "unrestricted" by the user.
  • Design response:
    1. Server-driven: push the time-critical event from the server via high-priority FCM instead of a local alarm only.
    2. Idempotent recovery: on every app start, reconcile local alarms from the DB (Q332).
    3. Telemetry: record alarm scheduled-vs-fired lateness by manufacturer/model, bucket, ignore-optimization status.
    4. User guidance: an in-app health check with a short explanation and a link to the app's battery settings (ACTION_APPLICATION_DETAILS_SETTINGS); vendor deep links are fragile, always guard with resolveActivity/try-catch.
    5. Escalate: if a vendor's behavior breaks a core flow, document it, and if the user base is large, engage the OEM or Google (device-compat program).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun openAppBatterySettings(ctx: Context) {
    val i = Intent(Settings.ACTION_APPLICATION_DETAILS_SETTINGS)
        .setData(Uri.parse("package:${ctx.packageName}"))
    try { ctx.startActivity(i) } catch (e: ActivityNotFoundException) { /* ignore */ }
}
// Telemetry: lateness = firedAt - scheduledAt, dimension = Build.MANUFACTURER

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hard-coding component names for OEM autostart screens: they break across ROM versions and may be rejected by Play.
  • Repeatedly nagging users.
  • Treating "works on Pixel" as done.
  • Using an unkillable "sticky" service hack; it burns battery and gets the app flagged.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can an app detect it is being killed by an OEM? → Not directly; infer via ApplicationExitInfo (API 30): getHistoricalProcessExitReasons shows reasons like REASON_USER_REQUESTED, REASON_LOW_MEMORY, REASON_OTHER plus a description string.
  2. Would a foreground service solve it? → Helps on many but not all OEMs, and Play restricts FGS use to approved types; not a general fix.
  3. How to prioritize which OEMs to handle? → By DAU share and incident rate per manufacturer from telemetry.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "ask the user to whitelist the app." Senior: treats it as a reliability engineering problem: server-driven delivery, recovery on launch, telemetry per OEM, honest UX, and ApplicationExitInfo for evidence.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fintech OTP-reminder feature failed for ~12% of users, nearly all on two Chinese-OEM brands; moving the trigger to high-priority FCM with a local alarm as a backup closed the gap.

questions.contextHtml: A habit app (600k DAU, 55% India) schedules a daily reminder with setExactAndAllowWhileIdle at user-chosen times. Support volume jumps: "reminder came 2-4 hours late or never". Analytics: scheduled-vs-fired lateness p50 = 3 s overall, but for Xiaomi/Redmi p50 = 4 min with 18% never firing, and Samsung p95 = 3 h. Crash-free rate 99.8%, no code change in the last 3 releases. The only recent change: marketing launched a campaign that doubled new installs. Logcat of a Redmi bug report shows the process was killed (am_kill ... reason: ...) after the user swiped the app away.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and what do you do this week and this quarter?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use setAlarmClock" or "add a foreground service." Both are policy-risky band-aids that ignore the evidence (swipe-kill, manufacturer skew).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the skew by manufacturer only, or also by new vs old installs (campaign users may never have opened the app twice, so Rare bucket)? Does lateness correlate with swipe-away? Is canScheduleExactAlarms() true for those users? What OS versions? Is a fallback server push available?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Send a server-driven high-priority FCM at the reminder time for the affected cohort (alarm stays as a backup, de-duplicated by reminder ID). Add an in-app one-time "reminders may be delayed" card for Xiaomi/Samsung users linking to app settings.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) OEM treats swipe as force-stop, so alarms were cleared; (b) Samsung sleeping/deep-sleeping apps after N unused days; (c) campaign users in Rare bucket with exact-alarm permission denied on Android 14; (d) Doze maintenance windows (but allow-while-idle should fire; red herring); (e) our own bug in rescheduling after update (rule out via release correlation).
  4.
