How I'd verify each: Query lateness split by manufacturer, bucket, permission state, and ApplicationExitInfo reason (API 30) gathered at next launch; repro on a Redmi: schedule alarm, swipe away, adb shell dumpsys alarm | grep com.example (alarm gone = cleared); on Samsung, put the app to sleep via Device care and compare; check the permission via appops get.
  5. Root cause: Platform guarantees stop at the AOSP model; the OEM layer cancels alarms when the user dismisses the app (and auto-sleeps unused apps). The campaign changed the user mix toward the devices where this matters.
  6. Fix: Short term: FCM backup + health-check UX. Long term: reconcile on every launch and on ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED; alarm-lateness telemetry by OEM with an alert; server owns the schedule; where the product category qualifies, setAlarmClock.
  7. Prevention: Device-lab matrix with Xiaomi/Samsung/Oppo; release checklist item "does it survive swipe-away and reboot?"; dashboard for lateness percentiles by manufacturer.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a sticky foreground service for a reminder (battery, policy); not undocumented OEM intents; not nagging dialogs on every launch. Backup push means server cost and dedupe logic.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The PM wants 100% reliability. → Say it's impossible on third-party-modified ROMs; offer a target (e.g. p99 lateness under 2 min on supported devices) and show the cohort data.
  • FCM isn't arriving either for some users. → Those are force-stopped or restricted; the only recovery is the next user launch, so show a missed-reminders list on open.
  • Could ApplicationExitInfo prove swipe-kill? → It reports REASON_USER_REQUESTED for user kills, but OEM cleaners often show REASON_OTHER/REASON_SIGNALED; combine with description text.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team ran an "OEM clinic" quarter: telemetry by manufacturer + FCM backup + settings guidance took reminder on-time rate from 78% to 94% without a single hack.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames devices or adds wake locks.
  • Hire: segments data, recognises swipe-as-force-stop, adds FCM backup.
  • Strong hire: telemetry design, dedupe, policy-aware recommendations and a reliability target agreed with product.

questions.contextHtml: A news app (2M DAU) prefetches articles via an hourly job and shows a "new for you" notification via silent FCM pushes. After an A/B test, the "returning after 3+ days" cohort shows: notification open rate -40%, "first load after open" p95 = 7.8 s (was 2.1 s). Server logs: FCM delivery to this cohort is 91% but device-side onMessageReceived count is 62% of sent. Job success logs show the hourly job ran 1x per day for these users. No change in app code; Android 13/14 majority; crash rate stable.
questions.promptHtml: Why does "sync stop after three days unused", and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Users uninstalled" or "increase job frequency." Higher frequency worsens quota use and doesn't change the bucket.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What bucket are these users in? Are pushes high or normal priority, and do they result in a visible notification? Are users force-stopping the app? Is the delivery gap uniform across OEMs? Did a policy change (target SDK) happen recently?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the pushes that matter visible notifications; collapse low-value silent pushes; show a cached "last good" feed with a freshness label to hide the cold load.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Rare/Frequent bucket: job quota (about once a day) and FCM high-priority quota cut the cohort; (b) silent high-priority pushes downgraded because they don't create user-visible notifications; (c) user-level restriction ("Restricted" battery setting) after a battery complaint; (d) data saver/OEM sleeping; (e) red herring: network quality.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log UsageStatsManager.getAppStandbyBucket() with every job run and push receipt; compare RemoteMessage.priority vs originalPriority; reproduce with adb shell am set-standby-bucket com.example rare then dumpsys jobscheduler to see the quota windows; check adb shell dumpsys deviceidle and FCM delivery report for dropped/deferred messages.
  5. Root cause: After a few days without foreground use, Adaptive Battery moves the app to Rare; the platform intentionally lowers job/alarm/FCM budgets for apps the user doesn't use. The design assumed Active-bucket behavior.
  6. Fix: Short term: server-side collapse and send fewer, visible, high-value pushes; reduce reliance on hourly background prefetch. Long term: prefetch on app open with a fast cached path; use ApplicationExitInfo and bucket telemetry to tune; consider notification engagement (open/interact) which lifts the bucket.
// Instrument every background run
fun logRun(ctx: Context, kind: String) {
    val b = ctx.getSystemService(UsageStatsManager::class.java).appStandbyBucket
    analytics.log("bg_run", mapOf("kind" to kind, "bucket" to b))
}
  1. Prevention: Bucket-segmented dashboards; a test matrix that includes Rare (am set-standby-bucket); policy: no silent high-priority pushes.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not exemption prompts (policy), not fake notifications to game engagement, not foreground services for prefetch.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can I programmatically move my app to Active? → No; only user interaction, notification interaction and certain system states do. Anything claiming otherwise is a hack.
  • App hibernation? → Android 11+ (API 30) hibernation applies after months (about 3) of non-use for apps targeting API 30+ (all apps from 12), revoking permissions and stopping background work; a different mechanism with a longer timescale than the 3-day drop.
  • What if the cohort is Restricted? → Treat background sync as unavailable and optimize the foreground path.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A feed team replaced hourly prefetch with a "first-screen from cache + server snapshot" design; perceived load for returners dropped 60% even though background freshness stayed bad.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases frequency or blames network.
  • Hire: identifies standby bucket and verifies with adb.
  • Strong hire: separates job quota, FCM downgrade and hibernation timescales; redesigns around foreground-first freshness.

questions.subtopic: Force stop vs swipe vs system kill
questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between the user force-stopping an app, swiping it from recents, and the system killing it for memory? What survives each: alarms, jobs, FCM, broadcasts, services?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many "background reliability" bugs are caused by assuming all three are the same. Senior engineers know the stopped-state model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On stock Android, swiping from recents only removes the task; the process may stay or be killed later, and alarms, jobs and FCM keep working. System (LMK/memory) kill ends the process but leaves scheduled alarms/jobs and pushes intact, and the process restarts on demand. Force stop (Settings > App info) puts the package in the "stopped" state: alarms, jobs and notifications are cancelled, services stopped, and the app receives no broadcasts (including BOOT_COMPLETED and FCM) until the user launches it explicitly. Many OEMs make swipe behave like force stop.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Event Process Alarms Jobs FCM Receivers/BOOT
Swipe from recents (AOSP) may live on kept kept works works
System kill (LMK / low memory) dies kept kept works works
Force stop (user or am force-stop) killed, STOPPED flag cleared cancelled blocked blocked until user launch
Uninstall/update gone cleared cleared token invalid n/a
OEM swipe-kill (some ROMs) killed often cleared often cleared often blocked often blocked
  • The "stopped state" (ApplicationInfo.FLAG_STOPPED) has existed since API 12: implicit broadcasts don't reach stopped apps; only an explicit launch (user tap or another app's explicit intent in some cases) clears it.
  • System memory kills follow oom_adj / process state; see the process-priority chunk. Cached empty processes die first.
  • Android 11+ ApplicationExitInfo records the reason. Test with adb shell am force-stop com.example (stopped state) vs adb shell am kill com.example (kill only if cached/background, no stopped state).
  • PendingIntent alarms registered before a system kill still fire and recreate the process.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// After process restart: why did we die last time?
val am = context.getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
am.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons(context.packageName, 0, 5).forEach {
    Log.i("Exit", "reason=${it.reason} desc=${it.description} ts=${it.timestamp}")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing with adb shell am force-stop and concluding "alarms are broken", when users rarely force-stop; or testing with am kill and concluding everything is fine.
  • Believing START_STICKY survives force stop (it does not).
  • Assuming FCM wakes a force-stopped app.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a foreground service survive swipe from recents? → On AOSP it usually continues (with its notification); behavior varies on OEMs, and onTaskRemoved is delivered to the service so I can clean up.
  2. How does an app leave the stopped state after install? → First explicit launch, since installed-but-never-launched apps are in stopped state (this is why BOOT_COMPLETED doesn't reach them).
  3. What does am set-inactive do? → Forces the app into standby inactive for testing, unrelated to stopped state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "swipe kills the app." Senior: uses the stopped-state model, can explain what each event cancels and why, tests accordingly and knows OEM deviations.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A navigation app's trip-end reminder worked in QA (swipe on Pixel) and failed for Oppo users, whose launcher force-stopped on swipe; telemetry via ApplicationExitInfo confirmed it.

questions.contextHtml: You own scheduling for a super-app (8M DAU, 70% mid-range devices, 40% of users on Android 10-12). Three features are being designed: (1) chat message delivery when the app is closed (p95 target < 3 s), (2) a daily 08:00 medication reminder (must be on time, safety-related), (3) a nightly photo backup of up to 400 MB on Wi-Fi + charging. The PM suggests "one foreground service for everything, keeps it simple."
questions.promptHtml: Pick the mechanism for each feature and defend it against the PM's proposal.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "WorkManager for all three" or "foreground service for all three." Both ignore latency, exactness, policy and battery cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a server (yes? then push)? Is the medication case regulated or just a convenience? Which Play category are we (alarm/calendar permitted for USE_EXACT_ALARM?)? Is the backup user-initiated?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); I'd first reject the single FGS: one permanent notification, Play FGS-type review, battery drain, and OEMs still kill it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (candidate choices):
    • Chat: high-priority FCM data message, then a short expedited job or short FGS to fetch/ack, notification displayed from the message.
    • Medication: exact alarm. Use setAlarmClock only if the app is truly an alarm/calendar; else setExactAndAllowWhileIdle with SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and fallback; plus a server-sent high-priority push as backup, and a reschedule-on-boot path.
    • Backup: deferrable job: constraints UNMETERED + charging + battery-not-low + storage-not-low; resumable chunks; WorkManager (A5) wraps JobScheduler; user-initiated transfer job (API 34) if the user taps "back up now".
  4. How I'd verify: Prototype and measure on a Rare-bucket low-end device: FCM p95 latency, alarm lateness under force-idle, job completion rate across a week; battery via Battery Historian / Perfetto power rails.
  5. Root cause of PM's idea being wrong: Mechanisms differ by guarantee axis: latency (FCM), time-exactness (alarm), deferrability with constraints (job); a FGS is for user-perceptible ongoing work.
  6. Fix (design):
Feature           Trigger                 Guarantee axis          Policy/cost
Chat              FCM high priority       latency, server-driven  visible notification required
Med reminder      exact alarm + FCM bkp   time-exactness          exact-alarm permission/category
Photo backup      job (wifi+charging)     deferrable, resumable   quota by bucket; no notification
  1. Prevention: Telemetry for each (delivery latency, alarm lateness, backup completion rate), kill-switch flags, per-bucket dashboards.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a perma-FGS; not polling alarms for chat; not setAlarmClock for non-alarms; accept that the backup may take several nights for Rare-bucket users, and surface progress in-app.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Backup must finish tonight for a premium tier. → Offer a user-initiated "back up now" (user-initiated data transfer job or FGS dataSync-class with notification), subject to the then-current FGS type rules (see chunk 08).
  • Chat on devices without Play services? → Fall back to a foreground connection while the app is visible and a polling job; accept degraded latency.
  • Cost? → Jobs/FCM are free; alarms are cheap; FGS has real battery and policy cost.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An architect killed a "keep-alive service" proposal by showing a week of battery vitals: the service alone made the app the top drain on 9% of devices.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one mechanism for all.
  • Hire: correct per-feature mapping with constraints.
  • Strong hire: justifies by guarantee axes, policy, OEM reality, adds telemetry and a degraded path.

questions.contextHtml: The team bumped targetSdk from 33 to 34 for 30% staged rollout. Within 6 hours: crash-free users fall 99.6% to 98.1%. Top crashes: (1) SecurityException: Caller com.example needs to hold android.permission.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM or android.permission.USE_EXACT_ALARM to set exact alarms (2) ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException from a receiver (3) MissingForegroundServiceTypeException: Starting FGS without a type. All are Android 14 devices. The release was approved because "tests pass on emulators with API 33".
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: causes, fixes, and process changes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back." Needed first, but it ignores that targetSdk 34 is mandatory for Play updates, so you must fix forward.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is rollout halted? Which of the three crashes has highest volume/impact on a core flow? Are crashes on fresh installs or upgrades? Which code paths call them (alarm, boot receiver)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt rollout; keep 70% on the old target; ship hotfix guards (try/catch + fallback) behind a feature flag if needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (by volume): (a) exact alarm without permission on fresh installs (denied by default for 33+ on 14); (b) boot receiver starting an FGS of a type not allowed from BOOT_COMPLETED (API 34/35 rules) or without the exemption; (c) FGS declared without foregroundServiceType and no matching FOREGROUND_SERVICE_* permission.
  4. How I'd verify each: Stack traces by API and install type; reproduce on an API 34 emulator fresh install; appops set ... SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM deny; adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED after su/with -p where permitted, or reboot a test device; check the manifest merger output for FGS types.
  5. Root cause: Behavior changes tied to targetSdk 34 (FGS type mandatory, exact alarm default-off for new installs, stricter background FGS starts) were exercised only on API 33 emulators; test matrix lacked a 34 fresh-install path.
  6. Fix:
// guards
val ok = Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < 31 || am.canScheduleExactAlarms()
if (ok) am.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(RTC_WAKEUP, t, pi) else am.setAndAllowWhileIdle(RTC_WAKEUP, t, pi)
try { ContextCompat.startForegroundService(ctx, i) }
catch (e: IllegalStateException) { /* ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException is API 31+ subclass */
    JobScheduler.schedule(...) }
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE"/>
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_DATA_SYNC"/>
<service android:name=".SyncFgs" android:foregroundServiceType="dataSync" android:exported="false"/>
  1. Prevention: A "behavior changes" checklist per target SDK, run before bumping; CI with API 34 fresh-install emulator; staged rollout gates (auto-halt at crash-free < 99.3%); canary 1% for 24 h; compat framework toggles in developer options to flip individual changes (adb shell am compat enable <CHANGE> pkg).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not catch-all try/catch hiding failures; not dropping to a lower target (Play deadline); not shipping a fix without test on a fresh install.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Exact alarm crash only occurs on fresh installs; why not upgrades? → Upgrading users keep an existing grant from the pre-14 default.
  • Can you test platform compat changes without raising targetSdk? → Yes, via am compat / App Compatibility Changes in developer options.
  • Is every one of the three crashes OS-version driven or targetSdk-driven? → The exact alarm denial default depends on OS 14 + install; the FGS type requirement depends on targetSdk 34; clarify per-case in the review.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A postmortem showed 11 target-SDK-driven incidents in 3 years; a one-page behavior-change checklist and API N emulator gates reduced it to zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rollback only.
  • Hire: identifies each crash with correct fix and fresh-install insight.
  • Strong hire: also delivers process changes (gates, checklist, compat toggles) and distinguishes targetSdk vs OS-driven behavior.

questions.promptHtml: Give me the timeline of Android's background-execution restrictions from API 23 to the latest, and the principle behind each step.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They test whether you understand why the platform tightens, so you can predict and design for the next change instead of reacting to crashes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each release moved control from the app to the system: Doze (23) and light Doze (24) batch idle activity; Background limits (26) restrict services and broadcasts; Standby buckets (28) rank apps by use; API 30-31 add hibernation, exact alarm and FGS-start restrictions plus expedited jobs; API 33-34 add the exact-alarm permission defaults, FGS types, and user-visible job types; API 35+ adds FGS time limits and boot-launch limits. The principle is: background work must be user-visible, deferrable, or server-triggered, and the cost of guaranteed execution rises each release.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
API (Android) Change Principle
19 Inexact alarms by default batch wakeups
21 JobScheduler system-scheduled work
23 (6.0) Doze + App Standby idle device saves power
24 (7.0) Doze on the Go (light), CONNECTIVITY_ACTION manifest limit cheaper idle
26 (8.0) Background service and implicit broadcast limits apps can't run freely in background
28 (9) App Standby Buckets, background Restricted setting usage-based budgets
30 (11) Hibernation (auto-reset for unused), ApplicationExitInfo, expedited jobs unused apps go dormant
31 (12) Exact alarm permission, FGS-start-from-background limits, notification trampoline limits exactness and visibility cost
33 (13) USE_EXACT_ALARM, FGS task manager (user can stop FGS), notification permission user sees and controls
34 (14) FGS types mandatory, exact alarm denied by default for new installs (33+), user-initiated data transfer jobs declared purpose
35 (15) dataSync/mediaProcessing FGS time limits, boot-launched FGS type restrictions (verify per type) bound FGS duration
36 (16) Job runtime quota changes and stop-reason refinements (verify against release notes) efficiency enforcement

(Items for 35/36 are less settled; confirm on developer.android.com behavior-change pages for your target.)

How to use it: before choosing a mechanism ask: Is the work user-visible (FGS/user-initiated job)? time-critical (alarm with permission)? server-triggered (FCM)? deferrable (job)? If it fits none, expect a future restriction to hit it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Feature-gate by capability, not just SDK_INT
val canExact = Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < 31 ||
    ctx.getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java).canScheduleExactAlarms()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Memorising versions without the principle, then failing on the next release's change.
  • Mixing up per-OS vs per-targetSdk behavior.
  • Assuming the latest doc applies to your min/target without checking.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What would you predict next? → More user-visible accounting (task manager, time limits), stricter quotas, and exact scheduling restricted to declared categories.
  2. How do you stay current? → Behavior-changes pages per API, Android Developers Blog, beta preview testing, and am compat toggles.
  3. What is your policy for targetSdk bumps? → Q347's checklist and staged rollout.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists Doze and standby. Senior: states the principle (visibility, deferral, server trigger), maps features to mechanisms, separates per-OS vs per-target changes and admits where facts need verification.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that mapped every background feature to "visible / exact / push / deferrable" in a spreadsheet absorbed the Android 14 changes with zero crashes; the neighbouring team without it shipped three hotfixes.
